[[RunningHead]]

Tribute to an Original

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

680 North Lake Shore Drive, Apartment 1201
Chicago, IL 60611

John Gedo  

Because Edgar Levenson arranged to cap the January 2004 interview with a long quotation from my assessment of the importance of his work, in this commentary I can only repeat myself. Nonetheless, I may now abandon the relatively nonpartisan tone I there adopted as a would-be intellectual historian of psychoanalysis: I believe that Levenson's conclusion that successful analyses result from imparting to patients hitherto missing cognitive and semiotic skills promises to revolutionize clinical practice. (Whether most psychoanalysts will be willing to listen to his message is another matter.)

Levenson has been telling us that all extant theories of psychoanalytic technique miss the heart of the matter. This is the explanation for the embarrassing fact that analytic effectiveness is unrelated to the theoretical views that guide the clinician. Without Levenson's explanation, it seemed as if success depended on the magic of a shaman—a situation that led numerous practitioners to view the analytic procedure as a sacred ritual, any departure from which relegated one to a nonanalytic limbo.

I have the impression that, in the course of the interview, Levenson tried hard to provide examples of how analysts may enhance their patients' cognitive and semiotic competence, to “reach levels of greater complexity and understanding” (if I may quote my own words). He also stressed that such efforts can only be carried out in the individual manner made available to each analyst by his or her cognitive and semiotic assets. These are the differences in “personality” that make the transactions within each analyst-patient dyad absolutely unique. Hence, analytic success cannot be reached by imitating the putative methods of admired predecessors. (I suspect Freud was keenly aware of these constraints, and that is why he refused to specify how he worked.)

In this view, the interviewers' repeated inquiries about what Levenson might do in various contingencies were misdirected; I assume that is why he told them what Tauber or Fromm or other respected luminaries might have done. Only the principles on which technique must be based can be taught, but these seldom came up for discussion.

Elaine Shabad  

The “WOLF” lurks in the shadows of our soul and in the depth of our unconscious. There he waits, ready to leap, swiftly and suddenly, to annihilate our fragile life. What is the nature of the “wolf” and when does it strike? How are we to grapple with its haunting potential to blindside one when least expected, to steal one's life, one's vitality, and those whom one loves most dearly? Sophia Richman courageously addresses these questions in her absorbing and moving memoir, which depicts her own history as a hidden child of the Holocaust.

A Wolf in the Attic is the story of Richman's life, formed by the gripping inscription of her earliest years. Before the age of three, she lived a shadowy existence in Lwow, Poland, with the “unthought known” (Bollas, 1989) that she and her mother were posing as blond Catholics with fictitious identities. Her father, an escapee from a concentration camp, was hidden in an attic from December 1942 until July 1944, when the Russians liberated Lwow. Sophia was given an edict by her mother, not unlike the warning Little Red Riding Hood was given by her grandmother in the classic fairy tale, to stay away from the attic door to avoid the “mean, hungry wolf: if you open the door, he'll get out and eat you up” (p. 45). This book is the story of Richman's earliest traumatic experiences, the recovery of unconscious memories, and their imprint on her growing-up years, her adult work life, and her most intimate personal relationships.

It is truly a gratifying experience to find a duet of two marvelous talents: one a world-renowned Japanese writer and the other an American who, with unyielding scholarship and abundant passion, explores the mystified psychological landscapes of the novelist.

Yukio Mishima killed himself in 1970 at the age of forty-five after having created voluminous novels, plays, and essays. He was an extraordinary talent, the kind of genius that comes along perhaps once in three centuries by “venturing places few have glimpsed and forcing readers to face their own darkness” (p. 2). Mishima made his debut at the age of sixteen, and paved his career quite successfully till the end. He also exhibited himself nude for eccentric and surreal photographs, and appeared in gangster films. He was acquainted with celebrities around the world and lived in a lavish European rococo mansion. A Response to Layton

Philip Cushman  

I am most grateful to Lynne Layton for her thoughtful and learned discussion of “Between Arrogance and a Dead End.” In that article I examined the pitfalls, respectively, of the right and the left in postmodern politics. Here, in my response to Layton's discussion, I try to sketch out and illustrate through clinical examples how, from the beginning, we might think differently about psychotherapy in order to avoid the excesses of both the right's monocultural arrogance and the left's moral relativism. Layton focuses mainly on the first error, which I appreciate. My overall point, however, is that the two errors can be effectively avoided only by attending to both at once, because ultimately they are expressions of the same philosophical problem and must be addressed in the same way: by a wholehearted embrace of a more fully thought out hermeneutic vision.

In her discussion Layton searches for ways of integrating into therapeutic practice realizations about how the larger institutions, arrangements, and ideologies of our social world shape psychological experience. That is a goal of mine as well. Being aware of the political influences active in the therapy hour—rather than trying to banish them—is a good thing to do because, well, there is no alternative. The interpretive turn has helped me realize that political activity is, always, present in the clinical hour. responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Levenson's Self

Irene Fast

Irene Fast

337 Lake Park Lane
Ann Arbor, MI 48103

Irene Fast  

Dr. Levenson seems both wary of and delighted with theoretical conceptions. On the one hand, it is a pleasure to watch his wily ways, in the unedited conversation, of evading his interlocutors' efforts to pin him down to one or another conception or technique. On the other, it would be difficult to think of another psychoanalytic scholar more broadly and seriously interested in theories. Korzybski, Piaget, William James, and Kuhn, among others, figure in his discussions, and he explores ideas originating in linguistics, general systems theory, the Tao and Sufism, Chaos Theory, right-brain—left-brain perspectives, and recent neurological approaches.

How can we make sense of this apparent contradiction? It appears to have to do with Dr. Levenson's high valuation of theory and, equally, his fear of its misuse. He sums up his concern metaphorically as the danger of confusing the map of theory with the terrain of the patient-therapist interaction. Theories are valuable as they offer new perspectives on that relationship. The danger is that instead of being one among many lenses illuminating the clinical situation, a theory becomes dominant, a Procrustean bed into which the patient must be fitted.

Self

This love of theory and fear of its misuse seem evident in one of Levenson's central foci of interest, the patient's self. He abjures any formalized theory of self. “I don't even know what ‘self’ really means,” he says. He finds that in the entire psychoanalytic literature there is not one single convincing definition of self. At the same time he titles his volume of collected papers The Purloined Self, and in the course of his writing he makes a wide range of observations about the self that suggest it to be fundamental to his thinking. As one might expect of him, these observations are firmly rooted in his clinical experience, modulated and expanded as he views that experience through the lenses of various theories.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Persistence of Layering Logic

Drive Theory in Another Guise

Bernard Apfelbaum PHD

Bernard Apfelbaum

2714 Telegraph Avenue
Berkeley, CA 94705

Bernard Apfelbaum  

defense, psychoanalysis, unconscious, ego, interpretation, interpersonal, insight

Even those who reject drive theory have had their thinking shaped by its conception of walled-off content. This inevitably generates a one-person psychology, despite the belief that working from a two-person psychology is a matter of choice. Drive logic, with its conception of fixed layers, is so intuitively compelling that it has obscured the way the (misnamed) structural theory conclusively invalidated it by conceiving of defense and defended-against as reversible, even as “in motion.” The revision requires a continuing differential diagnosis to determine what is defense and what is defended-against at any given time, one that rests on the patient's response and therefore is, of necessity, a two-person psychology.

My argument proceeds from early vignettes, followed by two contemporary case reports that can demonstrate the unrecognized continuing influence of layering logic in the understanding of dynamics and in inviting unyielding reliance on an interpretation, despite a patient's protests, the sine qua non of one-person analysis.

Arthur H. Feiner 1922-2005

Donnel Stern PHD

Donnel Stern

Donnel Stern  

Contemporary psychoanalysis was Arthur H. Feiner's journal, and in an important sense it still is. It was Art's baby, his pride and joy. The journal was founded by Max Deutscher and Rose Spiegel in 1964; but Art took over the editorship a few years later and held the job for a remarkable twenty-five years, from 1970 through 1995. He took the journal from its origins to its status as the international journal it has now been for many decades.

Art didn't have an editorial board to help him. He could have, of course, but he preferred to keep his hand firmly on the tiller. He had an enormous appetite for the work of editing. (Remember, most of Art's twenty-five years took place before the computer era. Even when the personal computer came of age, Art preferred to work by hand.) He sent manuscripts out for blind review, as we still do; but he was the one who received all those reviews and wrote all those letters to the authors of the manuscripts. He did almost all of the editing. (“Almost” because Darlene Ehrenberg served as his assistant editor for twenty years, and there were others, notably Clark Sugg, who made editorial contributions along the way.) Art made suggestions to writers about their manuscripts and sent the papers back and forth until they were ready to be published. The journal didn't have a copyeditor in those years. Whatever copyediting was done, it was Art who did it. He did everything.

Hard as he worked, though, Art's greatest contribution to the journal was not his labor, but his vision. He published writers whose work could not, and probably would not, have appeared in print otherwise. Some of these writers would have identified themselves as interpersonal and, eventually, relational; others would not have done so then and would not do so now. He established Contemporary Psychoanalysis as the open-minded, curious, multitheoretical publication that it is today. The number of significant psychoanalytic writers whose first paper, or first several papers, were published by Art is enormous.

William Alanson White Institute Wins Sigourney Award

Joerg Bose MD

Joerg Bose

Joerg Bose  

In November 2003, The William Alanson White Institute was named a 2003 recipient of the Mary S. Sigourney Award in recognition of the Institute's distinguished contributions to the field of psychoanalysis. The award, which includes a $35,000 grant, is made annually to individuals and institutions around the world, but only once every three years in the United States.

The award was founded by Mary S. Sigourney, who was born on November 30, 1927, in St. Louis, Missouri and lived for many years in Northern California. She was a resident of Carmel Valley, California at the time of her death from cancer on October 19, 1988.

Mrs. Sigourney had a passionate interest in psychoanalysis and wished to encourage activity in the field. Her interests included the contribution of psychoanalysis to other fields and disciplines such as psychiatry, psychology, child care, anthropology, sociology, law, criminology, and the arts and humanities. During her lifetime, she funded several academic research programs concerned with psychoanalysis and allied fields such as anthropology and sociology. She was a licensed psychotherapist and held a Masters degree in marital, family, and child counseling while receiving some analytic training and personal analysis. She was also the publisher of a Bay Area periodical, The Advocate, that covered environmental, social, and community issues.

Mary Sigourney understood the significant contributions of, and the lasting benefits from, psychoanalysis and its applicability to human affairs. She was concerned that establishment psychoanalysts were preserving a closed system of training and practice with insufficient attention to applied psychoanalysis and research. In instituting the annual award, now drawn from the Mary S. Sigourney Trust, she wished to encourage new activity in the field by recognizing outstanding contributions from individuals and institutions.

[[RunningHead]]

Secret Pleasures

A Discussion of Maroda's “Legitimate Gratification of the Analyst's Needs”

Sandra Buechler PHD

Sandra Buechler

154 West 70 Street, 10G
New York, NY 10023

Sandra Buechler  

We enjoy the ever-new fascination of traveling deep into inner space, both ours and the patients'.… One of my strongest and deepest reasons for wanting to be a therapist was that, ever since early childhood, I could think of nothing that gave me more intense enjoyment than listening to people telling me their stories.… We have the most interesting job in the world.

—N. Coltart, 1996

In naming some of the pleasures of analytic practice, is Coltart doing us a disservice? Are we better off concealing the gratifications our work provides, to protect ourselves from envy, jealousy, and public suspicion that we do not earn our fees?

In her paper, Karen Maroda argues for our honesty about what we derive from doing treatment. Like Coltart, Maroda believes in frank acknowledgment of the pleasures of an analytic life. Maroda (1991, 1998, 1999, 2002) has long been an ardent champion of the potential therapeutic usefulness of the analyst's deepest affective experiences. Once again, in this new contribution, we can recognize Maroda's unique voice, asking us to put aside fears of being misunderstood, or seen as narcissistically self-involved, and truthfully address our work's personal satisfactions.

Commenting on Gabbard's (2000) paper on the analyst's need for the patient's gratitude, Maroda suggests that we often settle for gratitude when our “deeper needs for self-healing and affirmation are not met” (p. 8). My comments address the nature of those deeper needs. What are the aspects of the human condition we most often bring to be healed by the treatments we conduct? Of course, any answer to this question is inherently subjective. In highlighting the roles of curiosity, hope, kindness, courage, the sense of purpose, a balance of emotions, the ability to bear loss, and integrity, I am naming what I ask of my own work.

389

Response to Sandra Buechler

Karen Maroda PHD

Karen Maroda

Karen Maroda  

I welcome Sandra Buechler's shared interest in the analyst's deep emotional experiences, which she has written about extensively elsewhere (Buechler, 2004). She is unabashed in her “romantic” view of the analytic process, favoring emotional experience over a rigid professional persona. I agree when she says that what gratifies us is both universal and unique to our own personalities, early experience, and training. I also agree that my paper would benefit from a deeper discussion of the meaning of “gratification.” I just simply couldn't figure out a way to attempt that discussion without digressing too much from the basic thesis I was presenting.

What I can add at this point, after reading Dr. Buechler's discussion and rereading the paper, is that I am talking about two essential levels of gratification. The first is the one required to keep the analyst satisfied enough with the relationship to stay engaged and actively participating day-to-day. The other level of gratification is the broader one that is the major thesis of my paper—that a similar, ongoing, transformative experience will necessarily occur within the analyst as it is facilitated for the patient. (The topic of the toxic patient or the toxic analyst who transform the other for the worse is yet another issue to be explored.)

Again, I am not saying that the degree of transformation will be equal to the patient's. I think a totally mutual transformation is unlikely, if for no other reason than that it is the patient's life that is the subject of the treatment. Yet I can honestly say that I have been significantly transformed as a result of treating certain of my patients, and am grateful for the experience. In other cases, I find the change in me is quite small. Some changes are dependent on the patient's presence in our lives, which may account for some of our reluctance to release certain patients and facilitate their terminations.

Buechler says she finds it helpful to consider the emotional impact her patients are having on her. “Are they easing my loneliness, increasing my curiosity about myself, making me feel less sad, or bringing me joy?” She also rightly notes that we may need different things at different times.

How do you Hold a Moonbeam in your Hand?**

Discussion of the Interview with Edgar Levenson

Marylou Lionells PHD

Marylou Lionells

939 Columbus Drive
Teaneck, NJ 07666

Marylou Lionells  

In this far-ranging interview we are introduced to the complexities and subtleties that characterize the mind and personality of a seminal thinker, a remarkable proselytizer for interpersonal psychoanalysis, who, more than anyone else, has been the poster boy for the William Alanson White Institute. Having this chance to express some of my impressions of and reactions to Edgar Levenson was an opportunity too good to miss. When I was a candidate in the late 1960s, Levenson was the star of the Institute, the most admired writer, the most sought-after supervisor. After I graduated, I found him constantly challenging his colleagues well-formed opinions and forcing us to rethink accepted canon. He elaborated Sullivan's theoretical assumptions, extended his clinical reach, and had the temerity to “analyze” Sullivan himself (Levenson, 1984). And when I became Director of the Institute he was often a welcome ally, but also, on occasion, a provocative reminder of the standards set by my predecessors. He is the unusual psychoanalyst-author who always found time to participate in administrative affairs, bringing his special perspective to the political and social as well as the intellectual life of the Institute. In what follows, I try to touch on these varied roles.

As Teacher

For several decades Ed taught an elective clinical seminar for White Institute candidates. When I took the course, each member was asked to present a problem case, one where the patient was incalcitrant or the analysis was stalled.

Along time ago, when I had the good fortune of being the editor of this journal, I invited Phyllis Grosskurth, who had written a splendid biography of Melanie Klein, to review Edgar Levenson's Ambiguity of Change (1983). I had sent her a copy, hoping that I would have an eloquent essay in my hands to grace the pages of the next issue. Her demurral detailed her time commitments and regrets, but also expressed that had she the leisure, she would love to meet with the author and discuss the things about psychoanalysis he seemed interested in.

Levenson has that quality of attractiveness. You want to meet with him, listen to him, talk over things with him, and then go back to the confines of your own consulting room, to muse about what he said, not necessarily in agreement, but in respectful contemplation of the consequences of the questions he raises, and their influence in your recognizing and then reorganizing what's going on with your work. For his is a coruscating fire-cracker of a broadly informed, most curious mind that raises questions, seeks no final answers in the therapy, only challenges, stimulating more and more questions, and hence, loosens up previously rigid ways of thinking, all in good humor and literate erudition. I hadn't met many, in my career in clinical psychology and at the White Institute, who could quote Groucho Marx, Wolfgang Pauli, and Confucius with equal ease, gusto, and aplomb. [[RunningHead]]

Paradigm Found?

Comments on the Levenson Interview

Joseph Schwartz PHD

Joseph Schwartz

2 Lancaster Drive
London NW3 4HA
U.K.

Joseph Schwartz  

As one would expect in a thoughtful, searching interview with Edgar Levenson, there is much to think about and respond to. His history at the White triggered my own memories of working there under Joe Jaffe in the late 1960s. His relaxed attitude toward scientific metaphors is such a welcome relief from what a colleague has called the Eureka shriekers, the “That's it!” at every scientific fad. And there are the little gems of clinical insight: higher levels of abstraction mean higher levels of anxiety—if you are looking to make sense of things in the consulting room, look to your countertransference, what's making you anxious? The list can easily be lengthened. All these threads are thought-provoking and open out, as he might say, into new material.

But I want to respond to something I think is quite fundamental in Levenson's description of the way he works and the way Hirsch and Iannuzzi respond to it. The theme I am responding to weaves through the entire interview. It is Hirsch and Iannuzzi returning time and again to questioning Levenson what he does in the consulting room—a search for principles or failing that, a desire for examples—“show us what you mean.”

Levenson, however, while being to my mind undefensive and open— in fact the open collegiality of this exchange is delightful—keeps telling them there is no principle.

For example, about countertransference: “And so what I think is irritating you about what I'm saying about the use of the countertransference—each time in each patient, I would do it differently. You're saying, ‘But there must be some principle’.”

And I think here we have the opportunity to explore what I think (in the first approximation without qualifiers) is the fact of the case: There Is No Principle.

Let me say it a different way.

717

Nestled in the urban forest of Toronto, Canada, a group of academics at York University is quietly revolutionizing how we think about alterity and the unconscious in education. Vibrantly situated in this group is Sharon Todd. In her latest book, Learning From the Other, Todd embarks on a philosophical and psychoanalytic investigation to understand the conditions that allow for ethical possibilities in education. The central theme in this book pivots around the idea that “we need to consider the ways in which ethics is something other than acting on knowledge” (p. 7). For Todd, this something other than knowledge is alterity and the unconscious. It makes perfect sense, then, that Todd turns to the work of the French-Jewish philosopher Emmauel Levinas and the notion of the unconscious to explore this topic. Although not prevalent in psychoanalytic writing, the ideas of Levinas address and enhance many concepts that are the foundation of psychoanalysis.1

Levinas, a holocaust survivor, spent his life attempting to understand alterity, the feeling or quality of being other, and “the inevitable responsibility each one of us has to the other we meet” (p. 2). Todd, expanding on Levinas's work, investigates “the conditions that make ethical attentiveness to strangeness possible in the first place” (p. 9). The term “ethics” is often used to describe what is good and bad, our moral duty and obligation; but, according to Todd, ethics are also “those moments of relationality that resist codification” (p. 9). This last definition of ethics speaks directly to the work of psychoanalysis, because analysts, too, spend time living out the moments of relationality (intrapsychically and interpersonally) that resist codification. This private experience, our otherness, when spoken out loud, is the foundation of every analytic encounter; it is where we begin learning from the other. Marc Maltz

240 West End Avenue, Ten A
New York, NY 10023

Marc Maltz  

change, trauma, consulting, organizations

This article explores a consultation to a financial services firm that lost 39 percent of its employees in the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. The consultation required both psychological and organizational work in a way that contributes to the evolving concept of the “organizational clinician.” This orientation leads to the conclusion that organizational consultants should be trained in clinical concepts (i.e., identity formation, transference-countertransference, and security needs) and that psychologists working in organizations should be trained in organizational development-systems concepts (i.e., mission, strategy, structure, performance, role, task, and authority). Cross-fertilization between clinicians and organizational consultants is especially necessary when working with organizations that have been traumatized or are experiencing change. This article reviews the work completed to help this firm's management, employees, and families grieve, recover, and succeed. It concludes with a look at the skills and competencies required to be an organizational clinician.

The Kinetic Transference and Countertransference

Frances La Barre PHD

Frances La Barre

666 West End Avenue, Suite 9W

Frances La Barre  

nonverbal, action, kinetic, rhythm, posture, movement, body

The author draws on movement theory and nonverbal research to show that there is a kinetic text, made up of all action and interaction, inclusive of speech action, that is as palpable and affecting as the verbal text. In this close description of a case, the author introduces the concept of the kinetic transference and countertransference, an aspect of the kinetic text and part of the overall transferential context of psychoanalysis. The author applies the theories and technical language of movement theory and nonverbal research to highlight the fundamental physicality of the psychoanalytic situation, and to bring this focus into the contemporary move to explore and comprehend action as an inevitable component of our enterprise. Through the author's report on the course of several treatment phases with one patient, she shows a level of practical convergence between nonverbal studies and psychoanalytic studies that, through the lens and corollary praxis of the kinetic transference and countertransference analysis, offers valuable leverage in psychoanalytic treatment.

Gay Men Tortured on the Basis of Homosexuality

Psychodynamic Psychotherapy and Political Asylum Advocacy*

Carol Pepper PHD

Carol Pepper

10 West 74th Street, LLD
New York, NY 10023

Carol Pepper  

The explicit integration of political asylum advocacy into the frame of psychodynamic psychotherapy is described. Patients are eighteen gay, bisexual, or transgendered men from twelve countries at various stages in the asylum process. Some are HIV+ or living with AIDS. All were persecuted or tortured in their countries of origin because of their sexual orientation. All are at risk of deportation if they do not win their cases. When they were children, several of the men were sexually abused. As latency-age boys and as older youths, most were physically abused because they were gender atypical. Technical recommendations regarding the process of asylum advocacy are provided. Advocacy and psychotherapy are not separate activities, but complex psychotherapeutic experiences. The therapeutic relationship is likely to become the crucible for intense feelings associated with childhood physical and sexual abuse, as well as subsequent persecution and torture. Both the therapist and the patient are vulnerable to acting in the transference-countertransference. It is possible that the necessary, asylum-related activity of the analyst in the early phases of the treatment will be negatively experienced by the patient at a later stage. Obstacles to resolving negative therapeutic reactions are discussed.

Donnel Stern  

Levenson's Place in Interpersonal Psychoanalysis

Hirsch, Iannuzzi, and Levenson are to be congratulated on this fine piece of work. It is more than I expected. Yes, of course, this interview is what such interviews usually are: it offers Levenson the opportunity to reflect on the field as a whole, interpersonal psychoanalysis in particular, and his own major contribution. But the interview accomplishes a good deal more than that. It doubles as some morphed form of scholarship. Hirsch and Iannuzzi are wonderfully well informed about Levenson's work, and they ask questions that allow Levenson to open up his thinking in ways that I am sure will surprise many of his readers. For his part, Levenson is articulate, collaborative, engaging, and forthcoming. The result is a document that, despite its length, grips us throughout.

This interview is the only time Levenson has ever tried to convey the sweep of his thought over the course of his career, and considering what we find out as he talks, it is high time for such a survey. Levenson's thought has developed over the years, and in ways that may not be obvious to his readers until they read this exegesis. For anyone who really wants to understand Levenson, this exchange has immediately become a necessary complement to his more formal published work.

But the biggest surprise in this interview is not its coverage of Levenson's ideas. No, it is Levenson's shockingly (yes, shockingly) inaccurate assessment of the impact of his own work. I can hardly believe that Levenson has so little idea of his own influence. He does say that he has always thought that The Fallacy of Understanding (1972) alerted Merton Gill, Lawrence Friedman, and some other prominent Freudians that interpersonal psychoanalysis was worth attending to.

Psychoanalysts may quote the physicist Werner Heisenberg at least as much as they do Edgar Levenson. Like Levenson, Heisenberg is associated with a revolution in his field, his “relativity principle,” contributing to the shift from classical physics to the modern world of quantum theory (Heisenberg, 1952). Fonagy (2001), for instance, credits Sullivan for traveling “halfway to Heisenberg” because he “put great emphasis on the analyst's participation in and impact on what he is observing” (p. 132). Similarly, Aron (1996), in questioning analytic neutrality, mentions that Heisenberg “demonstrated that the position of the observer and the acts of observation influence the nature of the data gathered” (p. 256). Much clinical case reporting is an enactment that alters, distorts, and reconstructs the analytic process and the analysand's experiences. The analysand's voice in clinical literature tends to disappear, leaving the analyst writer as the potential ventriloquist in an illusionary one-person psychic space. This paper presents a fragment of a woman's journey through analysis, hearing it in the patient's voice as it presents itself in an e-mail correspondence between the patient and the analyst. In this correspondence, the patient writes about her experience with her first analyst (to whom the correspondence is addressed) and with a second analyst who had found her to be unanalyzable (and with whom she is in analysis while writing). The first analyst, the patient, and the first analyst's colleague are exploring various actors' contributions to the analytic process.

The analysis of Peter is described, followed by verbatim process of one session. A life-long retreat into inner fantasy and the experience of himself and others as mere objects had enabled Peter to survive an upbringing in a boundariless, overstimulating, and punitive environment. The analysis focusses on helping this traumatized young man to feel that he can relate to others and maintain a sense of himself as coherent and alive. I am grateful for the opportunity to discuss Dr. Hirsch's and Dr. Iannuzzi's interview because, although I have known Dr. Levenson for a quarter of a century, the interview helped me to know him better. I first met Dr. Levenson in 1981, when I invited him to present his understanding of the Sullivanian paradigm to a meeting on “Models of the Mind,” sponsored by the American Psychoanalytic Association. In gratitude for his many contributions, I subsequently nominated Dr. Levenson for honorary membership in “The American.”

In contrast to the current interview, Levenson (1981) was very clear about his psychoanalytic theory. He stated: “I would claim that the clear line of schism between interpersonalist and Freudian remains the search for the truth behind appearances versus the search for the truth inherent in appearances. For the Freudian, the key question is what does it truly mean? For the interpersonalist, the question is: what's going on around here?” (Levenson, 1981, p. 53). Levenson emphasized in that paper that his understanding derived from Sullivan's (1956) view that “no one has grave difficulties in living if he has a very good grasp of what is happening to him” (p. 49).

In 1981, Levenson spoke from the perspective of revolutionary paradigm competition. In the ensuing quarter century he has shifted toward a more evolutionary perspective on the development of psychoanalytic theory. He states in the interview, “Part of what happened to me is it began to sink in after a while that the Freudians had something. You know, we were throwing the baby out with the bath water.” He continues, “I have a great appreciation of the Freudian perspective, because I think over the years it has been possible for me to think about it more.”

The interview is particularly interesting to me because in content it reflects the evolution of Levenson's thinking, while in form it seems to be paradigmatic of his therapeutic methodology. My reading of the interview is that it begins from the perspective of the interviewers' idealization of Dr. Levenson.

I recently played, for a psychoanalytic study group of which I am a member, a comedy sketch recorded ages ago, in which Elaine May and Mike Nichols portray a psychoanalyst and her patient. Having had a good laugh each of the numerous times I have listened to this sketch over the years, I gleefully, and as I now know naively, imagined my typically serious and scholarly group uncharacteristically doubled over, wiping tears of laughter from their eyes, enjoying a good joke on us all. In the sketch, the patient (Nichols) informs May, his analyst, that in the following week he will have to miss the last of his five sessions per week, since it is Christmas Eve and he plans to be with his family that day. Instantly shattered by the news of her patient's plan to desert her, May attempts to maintain her analytic stance and mask her spiralling self- fragmentation by demanding that her patient explore, be curious about, reflect on, and associate to his need to miss his session. In the face of his insistence that he just wants to be with his family on Christmas Eve, the analyst begins to weep quietly, then to sob in despair, then to scream with rage. Unable to help her recompensate, the patient quietly retreats, wishing her a Merry Christmas, as the analyst continues to unravel. When I turned off the recording, I faced a silent group, with some members finally confessing to a sense of excruciating anxiety while listening. There was little further discussion. We moved on quickly to the material we had planned to discuss. In showbiz parlance, I had bombed.

Hirsch: I want to start by saying that it's an honor for both of us to do this interview with you. As do many, we consider you the key interpersonal theorist following Sullivan, Fromm, and Clara Thompson—the Willie Mays or perhaps the Michael Jordan [laughter] of interpersonal analysts. Seriously, you are the key interpersonal theorist responsible for bringing interpersonal psychoanalysis from them [Sullivan, Fromm, Thompson] to contemporary times. Your uncompromising attention to the inclusion of the analyst's subjectivity has played a seminal role in laying the groundwork for opening up psychoanalysis to include the study of perspectivism, postmodernism, and for what's now widely called the “relational turn” in psychoanalysis. With that said, we feel there is a lot of ground to cover in the interview and so we decided not to focus too much on your personal life history. However, I would like to begin by asking what your personal reasons for becoming a psychoanalyst were?

Levenson: I arrived at it in a rather desultory way. I had gone to medical school, as a lot of middle-class Jewish kids did, because there weren't an awful lot of things one could do professionally in the 1940s. Once I got through medical school I really wasn't particularly sure what I was going to do with it, since I hadn't figured out what I was interested in really. At that point I went into the army for two years and was stationed overseas during the occupation. When I went in, I'd had a neurology residency, so the army gave me a neuropsychiatry specialty rating, and when I came out I was, mirabile dictu, a psychiatrist. I went on to get my boards in psychiatry, and then I went into analysis because I needed an analysis. In those days analysis was a little like syphilology in that it was okay to treat the disease but not to have it.

A Death Instinct Derivative?

Dori Laub

Dori Laub  

Through a detailed clinical vignette and a review of the relevant literature this paper illustrates the failures in narrative formation, symbolization, and even in the process of psychoanalytic listening and comprehension, that occur in the wake of events of massive psychic trauma. Inexplicable gaps and absences occur in what should be all too evident and readily known, and the processes of exploratory curiosity come to a halt. The author attempts to explain this phenomenon through the cessation of the inner dialogue with the internalized good object, the “inner thou” that is annihilated in massive trauma. He tries to demonstrate the role the death instinct derivatives play in this presumed shut-down of processes of association, symbolization, and narrative formation. Such death instinct derivatives come unleashed once the binding libidinal forces of object cathexis are abolished and identification with the aggressor (the only object left in the internal world representation) takes place. Implications for psychoanalytic psychotherapy with severely traumatized patients are discussed and illustrated by another case vignette.

Lewis Aron  

Interpersonal, interaction, relational, participation, technique, intervention, psychoanalysis

Contemporary psychoanalysts maintain a widespread consensus on the interactive nature of the psychoanalytic process. Mitchell (1997) compares and contrasts the clinical work of three well-known contemporary analysts from three different analytic traditions: Theodore Jacobs, Darlene Ehrenberg, and Thomas Ogden. Mitchell uses this exercise to demonstrate that we each have our own idiosyncratic styles of engaging the world, and thus it follows that we each participate in distinct varieties of analytic interaction.

This article places Mitchell's own clinical approach squarely in line with the interpersonal tradition. The article argues that among all of the various schools of psychoanalysis, the interpersonal approach is unique in the freedom that it gives to analysts to behave flexibly and spontaneously with interventions other than interpretation. The article comments on Mitchell's unique qualities as a clinician and teacher.

Harry Stack Sullivan, the founder of interpersonal psychoanalysis, was a gay man. His sexuality, far from being an incidental aspect of his life, was integral to his clinical and theoretical innovations. Sullivan was also a path-breaker in dealing with many aspects of gay civil rights that are still at issue today. Sullivan's writings about lust and sexuality have been difficult to understand and relatively ignored. When one decodes Sullivan's neologisms, one can appreciate how he was working toward a radical new formulation of sexuality's place in human living.

Daniel Gensler  

This book is a gem. It combines a masterly command of the literature on relational therapy and trauma, decades of clinical work with severely traumatized adolescents, the courage of a gifted therapist to tolerate

132

and use intensely difficult countertransference feelings, and good writing. I also feel a personal relation to some of the work described in the book. I served as director of the clinic where Cohen ran the longterm group for girls whose parents died or were dying of AIDS. I am glad that her work there became a central part of such an excellent book.

The trauma described in the book is substantial, arising from multiple severe stresses or ongoing traumatizing situations. The patients include teenage girls whose parents are dying of AIDS, Israeli army soldiers traumatized by exposure to death, and adolescents in inpatient units of mental hospitals.

For example, Cohen offers a vignette about Carmen, a fifteen-year-old girl whose father abused her mother throughout her pregnancy and abandoned her mother when Carmen was born. Her father remarried, was later imprisoned and then murdered, and her stepmother and baby halfbrother then died from complications from AIDS. Carmen's mother also developed AIDS. As a baby, Carmen smeared feces on herself, developed asthma, had delayed speech, and showed social and behavioral problems from a very early age. Physical and sexual abuse was suspected. When she was referred to Cohen, Carmen was anxious, angry, and hyperactive; she lied, stole, and destroyed furniture. This girl could not verbalize her feelings, and instead let her actions and stories show what she could not describe. Once, she brought an abandoned dog into the group session. She worried that if she left the dog on the street, it would die. She alternated treating it with love and with aggression during the session, a perfect screen for projecting and expressing her feelings about her own mother.

The book is organized into sections dealing with ways of surviving trauma, the evolution of the treatment relationship, and finding a treatment plan. The first section examines how traumatized teenagers cope with horror through the use of secrets, self-disclosure, enactments, dreams, and dissociation, with particular attention to cultural and social differences between therapist and patient. The second section proposes three phases in the evolution of the transference and countertransference between a therapist and a teenage patient. The first phase, engagement, involves resistance and an antitherapeutic alliance. Then there is a phase of safety, marked by signs of mutual tenderness, and a subsequent erotic phase in which the confusion between tenderness and sexual passion becomes central.

Aging, elderly, developmental issues, bias, psychoanalysis and mortality, life cycle, termination

The fantasied timelessness of unconscious experience collides head-on with the inevitable timedness of mortal existence. This is most palpable when working analytically with elderly patients and may help explain our need to avoid such individuals by labeling them as “inappropriate for analytic treatment.” Our cherished linear developmental models have often reified our biases into fact and permitted our own fears to remain inaccessibly active. When we analysts attempt to segregate elderly patients by denying them their analyzability, we succeed only in maintaining developmentally approved “them-not us” fantasies. This paper explores motivations for such fantasies, as well as the price paid by elderly would-be analysands, avoidant analysts, and psychoanalysis. Clinical vignettes are presented to assist in the deconstruction of such obstacles and their collusion with our reluctance to access experience and meaning at the end of the life cycle.

James Stoeri  

dissociation, surprise, shock, dread, trauma, enactments, creativity

The nature of therapeutic action is described in the experience-near terms of surprise, shock, and dread, and more theoretically in terms of dissociative processes. Dissociated experience is not available through the ordinary analytic process of uncovering and exploration because it cannot be reflected on and is inevitably incompatible with the treatment relationship as it stands. It can only find expression through enactments and, in the process, obliterates other perspectives or realities that are likely to have been hard-won by the analytic couple. I suggest that in the course of an analysis, when patient and analyst achieve deep mutual trust, a special set of circumstances evolves in which there is a change in the way the patient uses dissociation. The patient actively seeks out those aspects of the analyst's behavior or person that permit reexperiencing of the traumatic past and dissociates the other aspects of the analytic relationship involving confidence, goodness, and trust. This is not a defensive use of dissociation and in fact, if we know how to work with it, is potentially the conduit through which new experience becomes available within the transference. Working with it successfully entails the analyst encountering the shock of being altered in entirely unanticipated ways and the dread of it being permanent. A detailed case example is used to elucidate these ideas.

The author contrasts the classical psychoanalytic perspective on the relationship between culture, especially race, and transference with interpersonal and relational models. Recent developments in contemporary psychoanalytic theory provide a more comprehensive theoretical formulation of the relationship between culture, the unconscious, and the interpersonal field. The author takes the position that culture is an essential aspect of the transference-countertransference field, rather than something to peel away or move past in order to reach more deeply laden conflicts. Cultural transference-countertransference is constructed by patient and analyst together, and reflects interpersonal relations as well as internalized self-object representations. Transference-countertransference enactments between patient and analyst are conceived as embodying aspects of the historical relations between their respective cultures. While transference may have intrapsychic origins in the form of internalized self-object relations, it may also be a manifestation of a patient's sociocultural roots and family-of-origin's cultural heritage, including relationships to the dominant group. The author examines these ideas from a treatment between a white therapist and a black patient.

Buddhism, meditation, reverie, transcendent, embodiment, uncertainty, caesura

In examining an analytic encounter, the author's experiences with her analysand are understood within the matrix of intersubjective object relations, Buddhist psychology, and perinatal research. In the process of her clinical experience, the analyst experienced her body as a resonating, containing space, an echo chamber, to that of her analysand's unconscious communications. The author focuses on four capacities that foster a generative, bidirectional relationship between the conscious and unconscious, unconscious and unconscious, and between different self-states within and between analyst and analysand. These four capacities are mental flexibility, negative capability, unconscious reception, and intuitive capacities. With these four capacities in mind, the author formulates an intersubjective method she terms transcendent attunement, a fluid state of being in which occurs a transient and nonpathological suspension of duality between self and other and that constitutes an atemporal mode of experiencing.

Notes Toward a Nonconformist Clinical Practice

Response to Philip Cushman's “Between Arrogance and a Dead-End: Psychoanalysis and the Heidegger-Foucault Dilemma”

Lynne Layton PHD

Lynne Layton

253 Mason Terrace
Brookline, MA 02446

Lynne Layton  

Philip Cushman sounds a cautionary note for those who subscribe to the relational analytic paradigm, or to any other paradigm influenced by what he calls the “interpretive turn.” He wants us to take heed of the flaws in our philosophical mentors' lives and philosophies, and he spells out those flaws with care and balance. He also offers a way out of them: to redress Heidegger's arrogant monologism and monoculturalism, he prescribes Gadamer's correction to and extension of Heidegger's theory of authenticity, particularly Gadamer's emphasis on dialogue. Dialogue, he argues, counters Heidegger's disrespect for the interpersonal and social realm. To address Foucault's flaw—a missing moral perspective that might offer a counter to the abuses of power—he prescribes both Gramsci's theory of hegemony and Gadamer's theory of dialogue. Cushman argues that while Foucault's practice of genealogy opens us up to the recognition of difference, only dialogue enables us to do anything constructive with that recognition and to avoid nihilism.

I imagine that the occasion of Cushman's scrutiny of these theorists is that he sees something of those flaws operating within our own analytic theories and practices. Nonetheless, Cushman concludes that the therapeutic encounter is a privileged site of dialogue and, sadly, one of the few places left in our world where there is the good will for dialogue and the capacity to take on another point of view.

It is with regard to this sad state of affairs that I formulate my response, hoping not so much to critique what Cushman has to say, but rather to draw out some of the implications of his essay for clinical practice. Specifically, I want to think here about what a nonconformist psychoanalytic practice might look like.

E. Walker

20 West 86 Street, Suite 1C

E. Walker  

James Jones, who holds doctorates in both psychology and religion and teaches at Rutgers and Union Theological Seminary, begins his book by reminding the reader of the commonality of idealization across

567

all religious traditions, whether in the form of icons, symbols, or texts. In the mystical traditions of many religions, idealization is linked directly to romantic love, as the closest human equivalent of a psychological state of giving oneself over completely to God or some equivalent principle.

At the outset, Jones reiterates the claim made in his earlier book, Contemporary Psychoanalysis and Religion, (1991) that the relational turn in psychoanalysis provides a useful perspective for looking at idealization in religion by shifting one's view of personality structure away from instinctual determinants to the history of interpersonal encounters. In his current book, Jones develops this theme further, by detailing how he believes the interplay of idealization and one's history of interpersonal relationships creates a lens through which one experiences the sacred. He states, “relational themes echo and re-echo through our devotional practices, spiritual disciplines, cherished philosophical and theological convictions and our states of ecstasy” (p. 5). Along the way, he provides a refreshingly brief comprehensive review of how relational psychoanalysis from Fairbairn to Ghent views religious themes.

The core focus of the book is an excellent review of religious, psychological, and psychoanalytic perspectives on transformation. Jones points out that Freud viewed idealization as existing in opposition to reality testing: an idealized attitude toward one's parents must be overcome to come to terms with the reality of who they really are. Jones contrasts Freud's view of religion with Kohut's more positive one. In doing so, he presents the reader unfamiliar with Kohut with a challenge that is daunting, but ultimately rewarding.

Kohut, Jones explains, refutes Freud's contrasting of idealization and reality testing as it applies to both romantic love and the experience of death. Kohut insists that idealization and reality testing exist in a constructive polarity to enable the experience of healthy romantic love. His concept of self-objects requires an idealization of one's parents as a prerequisite for self-love.

Discussion of an Interview with Edgar Levenson

Lawrence Friedman MD

Lawrence Friedman

129 B East 71 Street
New York, NY 10021

Lawrence Friedman  

Even among psychoanalytic wise men we rarely find a vision trained specifically on the nature of treatment. A few heroes come to mind. The first committed treater was Ferenczi, and it is no disrespect to his foresight, courage, and experimental persistence to say that in later years he was guided more by how he wished treatment to work than by what he saw there. We can all think of a few brilliant therapists whose insights were blurred and blended in their charisma. Many others fell into the gravitational field of institutional loyalty. Many quickly patented an eponymous formula.

Human nature being what it is, we are all compelled to take part in the sociable chatter of our peers, but there are a few thinkers who are so intent on deciphering the mysteries of dynamic therapy that they let go of collegial concerns and wrestle with the mystery simply because it bugs them. For them it's essentially a private puzzle. Bewitched by the therapy puzzle, these single-minded questioners are open to every hint of an answer, but seem indifferent to the debate of the moment. I think of Leston Havens. I think of Merton Gill, seen in the light of his overall life work. We know there are others. But not many, I dare say, and some of them with no gift for—or interest in—writing, and therefore known only to their immediate circle. Narrowed down to therapy-obsessed investigators whose wondering is pure, whose gifts are singular, and whose way with words is a fair reflection of their genius for therapy (and I use that word carefully), we will not find a large crowd around Edgar Levenson.

It is not likely that Levenson would have been bewitched by any overarching, institute-sponsored theory. But he rightly gives the White Institute credit for its tolerance and pluralism and for not distracting him from his fresh and immediate experience of practice—indeed, even endorsing his quizzical focus on “what's going on around here.

I wish first to express my gratitude to the editor of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Donnel Stern, and to Irwin Hirsch and Victor Iannuzzi for the tremendous effort and obvious affection that went into this undertaking. I am also very grateful to Drs. Stern, Lionells, Friedman, Rothstein, Schwartz, Gedo, Fast, Maroda, and Feiner for their trenchant and varied commentaries on what has not been a particularly perspicuous body of work. 1

Largely, I did feel wonderfully elucidated, clarified, extended, and, mirabile dictu, understood. There are certainly minor issues that I would like to disagree with or clarify, but it feels to me not only caviling and ungracious to pick at such generous offerings, but really unproductive. I believe I have been more than fairly represented, and, if an author goes somewhere else with what I've said than I would have, so much the better. I am a great believer in—and practitioner of—Harold Bloom's concept of “misprision” i.e., the unwitting, creative misreading of a previous author (Bloom, 1973; Feiner, 1977, 1988). I would be flattered to be the jumping-off point of someone else's originality.

One small point: Dr. Maroda regretted the lack of personal disclosure in the interview. I would remind her that, out of time considerations, it was the decision of the interviewers to limit personal inquiry. I did contribute a more personal perspective to Reppen's compilations of psychoanalysts' histories (Levenson, 1998).

I do wish, however, to elaborate on what has been commented on as my modesty. I never considered humility as among my more prevalent shortcomings. But, it is true, I am quite diffident and uncomfortable about discussing what I have written. Consistent with my concept of resonance and enactment, I believe that I arrive at what I write very much as I arrive at clinical insight. Psychoanalysis and religion got off to a famously bad start. Freud viewed religion as the foe of science and reality, and he saw humans as all too easily seduced, sedated, and subjugated by religiosity. A century after Freud's initial attacks, many of us may not be aware that a psychoanalytic war against religion is still going on in some quarters. Or perhaps we have tacitly accepted the Cold War that set in at about the time of Freud's death in 1939. Even those of us who never adopted the once standard psychoanalytic posture of atheism, as a hallmark of intellectual and even moral superiority, may nevertheless be working behind a kind of Berlin Wall, carefully segregating, for ourselves and our patients, our spirituality from our psychoanalysis.

With the publication of Minding Spirituality that wall comes tumbling down. In meticulous detail, backed up with first-rate scholarship, Randall Lehman Sorenson makes it clear that it can now be officially declared: the war between psychoanalysis and religion, both the hot and the cold, is over. Sorenson titles his ultimate chapter “Psychoanalysis and Religion: Are They in the Same Business?” and follows with this:

Obviously not. The history of religion and science is one of chronic warfare, with religion on the losing side due to the steady advances of secularization. Religion is about belief, science is about practice, and psychoanalysis, like any science, therefore has little in common with religion. It is a different business. [p. 143]

Analysts use self-disclosure as a way to feel connected to patients without feeling overly revealed. Using her personal experience of closing her longtime practice and relocating, the author examines what she told to patients about her reason for leaving and what she knowingly or unknowingly kept to herself. Although she was very aware of her need for connection during this difficult time, she was less conscious of her need for privacy. As a result, she did not consider what she omitted from her disclosure or why, and ended telling her patients only partial truths. Analysts need to remain aware of their need for both connection and protection in their self-disclosures and, more generally, in their theoretical orientations and their day-to-day functioning as analysts.

Stephen Hartman

Stephen Hartman  

In the existential-phenomenological tradition, understanding oneself is not a matter of reflecting on one's encounter with the world, but of experiencing that encounter in all its fullness. To discover that we are human entails finding that inevitable “surfeit of meaning that cannot be reduced to the context or constructs we use to explain individual experience” (Frie, p. 18). An embodied experience of self lies at the core of all understanding. Roger Frie writes: “we determine our worlds just as our worlds determine who we are” (p. 18). In Understanding Experience he has assembled a very scholarly collection of papers to show how this premise is born out in different theorists' and clinicians' work.

Frie and his colleagues situate their writing in a critique of postmodernism. They believe that postmodernists' preoccupation with language, context, and the social construction of intersubjectivity proffers a dangerous turn away from the self who experiences back to the subject who thinks. Determined entirely by his context, the postmodern subject only understands himself by deconstructing his situation, that is, by thinking about it. Since postmodern theory emphasizes that our thoughts are largely structured by discursive regimens and relational configurations, even the most thoughtful person takes second place to context. The practical implication of this for clinical work is that explanation trumps experience. Postmodernist clinicians end up tracing multiplicity while having no way to engage real selves.

It will be immediately clear that I do not agree.

Between Arrogance and a Dead-End

Psychoanalysis and the Heidegger-Foucault Dilemma*

Philip Cushman PHD

Philip Cushman

17804 Thorsen Road, SW
Vashon Island, WA 98070
lobelia1@att.net

Philip Cushman  

The interpretive turn in the human sciences has profoundly influenced interpersonal, postmodern, and now relational psychoanalysis. Although it has transformed psychotherapy theory in many ways, some important philosophical difficulties have also followed in its wake. In this paper I examine two founders of the interpretive turn, the hermeneuticist Martin Heidegger and the postmodernist Michel Foucault. Practitioners of both theories feature an understanding of human being that is historical or cultural, and yet, admirably, attempt to avoid historical determinism. Some hermeneuticists do so by emphasizing how historical traditions intersect and then affect one another; some postmodernists do so by emphasizing the experiential and heuristic importance of the sociopolitical periphery. I examine these two strategies and their implications for psychotherapy by critiquing Heidegger's involvement in National Socialism and Foucault's limited vision of the moral: Heidegger's monocultural arrogance and Foucault's extreme relativism. I argue that both positions are deficient, and suggest that Hans-Georg Gadamer's hermeneutic concept of dialogue (enhanced with some of Antonio Gramsci's socialism) can remedy both flaws and point the way toward more helpful psychotherapeutic applications of the interpretive turn.

Karen Maroda PHD

Karen Maroda

825 North Jefferson Street, Suite 325

Karen Maroda  

Perhaps no topic is more controversial than that of the analyst's needs being met in the course of treating the patient. Prior emphasis has been placed on satisfaction derived from the patient's progress, with frequent warnings regarding the analyst's inappropriate pursuit of her narcissistic needs. The author readily acknowledges that all manner of inappropriate gratification does exist and harms both analyst and patient. Yet the major thesis presented in this paper states that mutuality is a driving principle in all human relationships. If this is true, then anything that is essentially harmful to the patient is also harmful to the analyst. But it also means that if the analytic relationship facilitates self-discovery and therapeutic transformation of the patient, while providing a sustaining level of affirmation, safety, and well being, similar benefits will occur for the analyst.

The Grammar of Irrationality

What Psychoanalytic Dream Study can Tell us About the Brain*

Mark Blechner PHD

Mark Blechner

145 Central Park West
New York, NY 10023

Mark Blechner  

rrationality, primary process, dreams, brain damage, interobject, disjunctive cognition, neurobiology, transference, reality

Not all kinds of irrationality are equal. The comparative study of dreams, brain damage, and psychopathology can reveal the “grammar of irrationality,” the rules of what can and cannot happen in various states of consciousness. We may then modify and refine the properties of the “system unconscious” described by Freud (1915). Examples are provided of “disjunctive cognitions” and “interobjects” which suggest constraints on the irrational combinations and distortions that are possible in dreams. Further exploration of these phenomena and their underlying neural mechanisms may help clarify the neurobiology of transference. Unusual experiences of nested reality in dreams suggest also that reality may be a quality that our minds can apply to an experience. We should study not only “reality testing,” but also “reality assignment.”

James Fosshage  

Abstract: I discuss Dr. Robert Grossmark's Case of Peter from a self-psychological/relational perspective. Peter's is a story of a man with remarkable determination and resilience and of a highly facilitative analytic dyad. Having come from a family experience of extreme parental abuse, Peter was able to self-regulate, generating fantasy selfobects to survive on his own. At a time of crisis he approached psychoanalytic treatment with expectancies of distrust. A good match in intelligence, intellectual values, and humor, Dr. Grossmark highlighted the repetitive self and relational themes and picked up the “leadingedge” (what the patient is striving for) of the material. Through his explicit-declarative focus (analytic inquiry) Robert interacted with Peter in a reflective, noncontrolling manner that, in turn, Peter experienced as respectful and promoting, cocreating new implicit relational learning.

Evelyn Hartman  

Intersubjectivity is a construct used to describe the relational dimension of the psychoanalytic process. Its definition may vary depending on the specific theoretical and philosophical tradition to which it is applied. The particular understanding of intersubjectivity espoused by Buirski and Haglund in Making Sense Together is founded on two assumptions: “that our subjectivity (our moment-by-moment experience of ourselves and the world) emerges within a dynamic, fluid context of interfacing subjectivities, and that we can never completely bracket our subjectivities to observe things as they really exist” (pp. xix-xx). One's subjective experience is made up of patterns based on repeated emotional experience with parents and caregivers (Orange, Atwood & Stolorow, 1997). In the words of the authors, “A central organizing concept of intersubjective theory is that our experience of ourselves is fundamental to how we operate in the world. Our subjective experience is the phenomenology of all that one might be aware of at any given moment and much of what is out of awareness, as well. Over time, the complex interweaving of individual abilities and temperament, relational configurations with caregivers during infancy and childhood, and the lucky or harsh realties of one's life circumstances converge to form patterns” (pp. 1-2). The need to maintain patterns, these organizations of experience, is the source of human motivation (Stolorow, Atwood & Brandchaft, 1994). In treatment, we hope to understand these patterns in the context of a relationship that becomes a new lived experience and the basis of new organizing patterns.

Gilead Nachmani  

Since the late 1960s and early 1970s a genre of nonfiction literature has emerged—first person narratives about bearing witness to horror. The authors tell how they survived massive genocidal trauma. This can be seen in the work of Terrence Des Pres who described in detail a certain kind of person that he called a survivor, one with singular skills that permit him to carry on in the face of catastrophic life-threatening events. This literature gained in popularity through the works of Primo Levi (1986), Alexander Solzhenytsin (1963), Yevgeny Kogon (1982), and Jacobo Timmerman (1987). It is characterized by an obsessive attention to detail by a narrator writing in the first person. At times it is repetitive, and seemingly has too much memory for the reader to absorb, but not more memory than the narrator has to offer (Zuckerman, 1993). It is as if the executive editing capacity of the narrator is somewhat lacking.

At times the text is so graphic that readers cannot help but feel they are invading the author's privacy, and at other times that the author is invading the reader's privacy. The author bears witness and gives testimony. In contrast to the vivid details, there are also gaps in the narration due to a traumatic loss of memory. At times, a glaring lack of affect accompanies vivid scenes of sadness. It is as if the feelings have been replaced by abundant detail. It is not uncommon for the reader to become uncannily overwhelmed by a sense of intrusive, claustrophobic anxiety from within the self. These stories evoke powerful and passionate responses in the reader, who can be awe-inspired by the courage of the author who reaches out from hell, using the beauty and civility of words to engage him. The authors are using narration in an attempt to transform unspeakable atrocity into mentionable tragedy. In doing so, they evoke powerful empathic reactions in their readers.

During my first year of training in analytic group therapy, I felt my work with adolescent groups was never taken seriously except by my supervisors. My classmates seemed to think that this work was not intellectually challenging, that it was not very sophisticated, and that it was not“real analysis.” I felt dismissed and ignored, and that the only way I could be taken seriously was to lead an adult group. I have since learned that my experience was not unusual. Many therapists who work with adolescents report feeling like “second-class citizens”in the psychoanalytic community. Furthermore, therapeutic work with adolescents as a distinct developmental stage has been largely ignored in group theory.

When Genders Collide

Dissociated Anger between the Female Analyst and Her Male Patient*

Ruth Livingston PHD

Ruth Livingston

330 West 38 Street, Suite 910
New York, NY 10018

Ruth Livingston  

anger, hate, dissociation, countertransference, gender, attachment, maternal

This paper adds to the growing but still sparse body of psychoanalytic literature that explores the role of gender in transference and countertransference enactments. The author contends that gender inscription can create a kind of conflict of interest between certain female analysts and certain male patients, especially around attachment, autonomy, and authority. The result may be an undercurrent of anger in which both participants in the analytic dyad dissociate. Here, the focus is on how one female analyst found she dissociated anger because of internalized stereotypical gender restraints, and how her male patients likewise dissociated their anger at her. Using material from her male patients and attuning to her own personal experience, the analyst illustrates how she and her patients were ultimately able to acknowledge their angry feelings and then transform them into a more authentic and mature, hence therapeutic, dialogue.

John Fiscalini  

Recent “postmodern” developments in psychoanalytic theory and practice have swept into analytic view yet another look (and study of) fundamental questions of agency, freedom (of will), personal responsibility, authenticity, and the nature of truth and analytic authority. This epistemological upheaval forms the central concern of Roger Frie's interesting new book of edited essays on human experience and psychoanalytic theory.

The so-called postmodern turn in psychoanalysis, as in such diverse fields as architecture, critical theory, contemporary art, and philosophy, has led to the questioning of our fundamental beliefs. For analysts that, of course, means our concern with the nature of that human encounter we call the psychoanalytic process. Frie's book serves as an excellent guide through the philosophic, intellectual, and clinical thickets of post-modern thought and belief. The illustrious contributors to this volume, individually and jointly, help us achieve a more sophisticated and complex understanding of the dynamisms that make up the analytic process. This book is more than just another entry in the debate between the “old” positivism of modernists and the “new” relativism of postmodernists.

Irwin Hirsch appears to be on a mission—to interview famous senior analysts and ask them to tell the truth about how they really work. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the secrets of the great analysts can be teased out, and perhaps duplicated by those who seek mastery. I applaud Hirsch's efforts and admire his tenacity. I do not sense any intention other than an honest desire on his part to discover more about how master analysts work, and to pass this information on to the next generation. Easier said than done. This interview with Edgar Levenson is his second in what I hope will be an ongoing series, in spite of the fact that the subjects are impossibly elusive on the topic of how they work.

Hirsch's first published interview was with Benjamin Wolstein and appeared in this journal five years ago (Hirsch, 2000). I participated in the discussion of that interview (Maroda, 2000) and was bowled over by Wolstein's easy commentary on himself and the analytic world, even if he did resist Hirsch's repeated attempts to talk about what he actually says to patients. I had found Wolstein's writing to be difficult to read and understand. So I was very pleased and grateful for Hirsch's eye-opening interview with him, which demonstrated a clarity of thought and purpose that, to my mind, never evidenced itself in his writing. He was so present and engaging that I found myself developing an attachment to him as I read the interview and wishing I had met him before he died.

So when Donnel Stern asked if I would participate in discussing this interview with Edgar Levenson, whose work I have read, studied, and cited over the years, I jumped at the chance. Given how readable his writing was, I eagerly anticipated getting a candid and personal reflection by Levenson. I have never met him, so I looked forward to “meeting” him in the way I met Wolstein—through the medium of Hirsch's interview. I expected an in-depth and revealing portrait of him would emerge from the questions posed by Hirsch and his cointerviewer, Victor Iannuzzi. I was wrong.

Love's Labor**

A Review of To Redeem One Person is to Redeem the World: The Life of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann by Gail A. Hornstein. New York: The Free Press, 2000, xxxii + 478 pages.

Carol Pepper PHD

Carol Pepper

10 W. 74 Street

drcpepper@aya.yale.edu

Carol Pepper  

Readers of Contemporary Psychoanalysis are likely to be fascinated by Gail A. Hornstein's engaging and comprehensive life of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, M.D. (1889-1957), the psychiatrist-psychoanalyst whose legendary work with psychotic patients at Chestnut Lodge in Rockville, Maryland, and whose book, Principles of Intensive Psychotherapy (1950), made her a widely celebrated and at times harshly criticized analyst and teacher. She was a cofounder, with Dexter Bullard and Harry Stack Sullivan, of the Washington School of Psychiatry, an original member of the core teaching faculty of the White Institute, a past president of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, and the fictionalized “Dr. Fried” in Joanne Greenberg's novel, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden (1964).

This biography is captivating, largely as the result of its source material. Because of World War II, next to nothing survives in Europe to document the first forty-six years of Fromm-Reichmann's life. Hornstein interviewed Fromm-Reichmann's only surviving relative, her niece, Alisa Jacobson Fuchs, and listened to a set of autobiographical reminiscences that Fromm-Reichmann audiotaped the year before her death. She was able to review extant letters, drafts, notes, records, and audiotape recordings, written or spoken by Fromm-Reichmann or sent to her. Over a period of five years she immersed herself in the offices, basement, attic, and storerooms of Chestnut Lodge, studying Fromm-Reichmann's clinical work in multiple forms—progress notes, tape recordings, verbatim transcripts of psychotherapy sessions, case conferences, clinical notes, and correspondence. She interviewed Joanne Greenberg extensively. She got to know former members of the Chestnut Lodge staff, the nurses, Fromm-Reichmann's secretaries, many of her friends. In all, she devoted more than a decade of her life to the research and writing the book required.
